transcription: At the end of the rainbow, please review, most kids walked by the stop sign and Bardem Street without noticing the do that rested on its base. But Phoenix always stopped. Water, he believed, never arrived without reason. Every morning, as the morning sun begins its small climb, Phoenix notice the beads of dew cling quietly to the surface of the stop sign. They seem frozen at first, as if listening to the waking world. Then, gently, gravity stirs them. Phoenix sat on a bench near a stop sign and quietly observed the do that pooled at the base. He pulled a sketchbook from his bag and drew a sketch of what he saw. As the dew moves, it leaves a glistening trail, he thought. Maybe dew isn't water at all, he wrote, but early morning messages sent in code. Phoenix sat still, watching each droplet ease its way down the smooth surface. You're at it again, set a familiar voice. He turned to see gale, hair toweled, uneven socks, messy laces, and his bag barely hanging on his shoulders. It's dew, Phoenix said, not looking away. It's moving slower today. Or the sun isn't warm enough yet. Gale sat beside him, or maybe you're looking at it from the wrong angle. Or the humidity's changed, he paused, or maybe you're just really into damp metal. Phoenix grinned, maybe. Or maybe the universe is leaving clues gale rolled his eyes, fondness softening the motion. As if he'd heard it all before, clues for what? I haven't figured it out yet, Phoenix said, but I will. Bring the bell echo down the street. Gale nudged Phoenix, time to stop decoding dew, with a smirk on his face. Phoenix sighed, closed his sketchbook, and slit a pencil behind his ear. They turned toward the school gates. Gale adjusted his bag for the third time, it kept slipping no matter how tightly he clinched it. You ever think about getting a new bag? Phoenix asked without looking na, he grinned, we've been through a lot, this bag and I loyalty counts for something. Phoenix smiled but said nothing. The classroom smelt like chalk dust and last week's wet socks. Phoenix slid to his seat near the window, and Gale sat next to him. Ms. Trenholm, their science teacher, paced at the front. Today, she said, with a stern look of someone who believed curiosity had limits, we're revisiting water cycles. Vapor, condensation, precipitation, no rainbows, no unicorns, just reality. But isn't a rainbow technically part of water cycle too? I mean, it's light and moisture and angle, right? Phoenix, sitting up straighter. A few students turned in their seats. Ms. Trenholm raised an eyebrow. Rainbows are illusions, Phoenix. Optical phenomena. Not scientific gateways. Phoenix blinked. But what if there's more to it? My dad said we're not discussing meteorological fiction. She cut in, her lips thinning. Stick to what's in the textbook. Gale glanced sideways and nudged Phoenix's notebook. Quietly, he whispered, you want to draw the water cycle with wings? Phoenix smirked. He flipped to a blank page. After a long day of school, Phoenix grabbed a ladder, his sketchbook, and a broom. He set the ladder up in the middle of the passageway and used the broom to open the attic door. The attic was dusty and it old wooden floors. The dust was why Phoenix loved the attic. He wanted to observe it and jot down what he saw. He entered the attic, and left the door a little ajar, blew the dust off of where he would sit and began observing. He sat there, looking, for a good 10 minutes. Phoenix's eyes widened as he traced the patterns of shimmering dust, swirling in the beam of afternoon light, each particle echoing the secrets of forgotten days. As he moved to grab his sketchbook, his elbow brushed against something. He turned his head and saw a metal box that had accumulated dust he blew off years of dust. The metal box trembled as he opened it. Inside was a document placed near a prism. Chromatic refractive studies, research Phoenix's father had been doing about the rainbow. His father theorized that the rainbow could, possibly, be harnessed or predicted. A prism does not create a rainbow, it reveals it. Phoenix reached for the prism, squinted his eyes and slowly started rotating the prism seven distinct bands visible, changing slightly depending on ambient humidity. Woh wonder, wonder was born. Time froze as he held the prism, the faint hum of the attic faded into the background. He'd always seen the rainbow but this was the first time he'd noticed it. A faint heartbeat echoed in this ears. This wasn't just research but a search for something beyond the ordinary. Honey, dinners ready his mother called. Coming he hastily placed the prism in the metal box, shut it, and left the attic. So, how'd school go? His mother asked. Good, like always trying to hide the grin on his face. Anything new today? I looked at the morning due today, he said, I was going to wait till it evaporated but class started. You know, morning due forms from when water vapor in the air condenses into liquid droplets on cool surfaces, dad started yet, it's water vapor's way of saying hi, mom said, you wouldn't know of its presence if it didn't leave morning due. When the family was done with dinner, Phoenix's mother cleared the table. Don't forget to get the ladder ready, Phoenix she called out while the boy was fetching the ladder from the hallway, his father was getting a blanket. Every night the family gathered on the roof. Under the vast, star-studded sky, they unfurled the blanket and settled down. A light breeze carried a scent of cool grass and distant memories.
